## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

and each is built on the public facts named here.

the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why7: The rungs are one measure in the right order, with a working rung above the line and four shortfalls below it, but the last rung swaps the outcome in for the measure, which is the very 'simply lost' stand-in the card warns against.
screens.instead: Keep the first four rungs and make the last 'None were ever called back', with the line under 'Every missed call called back within the hour'.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my questions belongs right before the study goes out to reservation agents, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question and hint are clear, but 'Lock and record the face Keel preselects' needs a second read: I don't know what 'lock' means here or whether 'record' means Keel films something now.
screens.why3: This is my own decision as the founder about how my study is delivered, so I can answer it directly.
screens.why4: The picked option is the odd one: 'lock and record' mixes accepting the default face with a recording step I didn't ask for, and it doesn't say whether the face speaks German to agents in Munich.
screens.why5: Nothing about Codyco, the AI receptionist or my roles appears or drifts; the screen is only about the interviewer.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, and in which language? (Use the interviewer Keel picked, in German / Pick a different interviewer / Record yourself asking them)

screens.why1: Once I've said who sends the questions, the next thing to settle is how my reservation agents take them, so this belongs right before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Talking on video, typing or tapping are plain to me and to an agent between calls; Daphne is explained in the same line.
screens.why3: I know my agents answer on a busy desk with a headset on, which is why I picked read and tap, so I can answer this from my own trade.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real choices (voice, text, or both), and none is missing or odd.
screens.why5: Nothing about Codyco's AI receptionist leaks into the format choice, and my pick of Read and tap stands as I made it.

screens.why1: Once the study is set and the answer mode chosen, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Short, plain options I read at once; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own UI word but explained by 'from a search'.
screens.why3: I know whether I have named reservation agents at the hotel groups I work with or would post in a hotelier group, so I can answer from what I do.
screens.why4: Three distinct, complete routes (named people, a Keel search list, an open link to a group) with no overlap, and my pick, people I know by name, is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed or leaked; the screen is about distribution only.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title with '4 beliefs: 4 holding · 7 people answered' beside it, and the rule 'the verdict is the worst of all its cards' ties it to the card numbers.
screens.why_b2: Each card says what was counted, over 7 and where my bar sits ('7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7'), but the Importance card prints '6 of 7 put it in their two' twice, so I had to look again to see whether that was one count or two.
screens.why_b3: The names and the Prevalence, Frequency and Current solution lines are mine; the Importance line grafts my whole circumstance into 'five things that are hard when booking calls come in... and not every one gets answered', which I recognise but would never say.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what four holding beliefs mean for Codyco or what to do next; the only closing text, 'What it measures', explains the rule, not the next move (for example, go read the commercial stage or book pilots).
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every card and 'Holding up' is a modest word, but nothing says seven agents is a small sample, and my 'seven-figure rounding error' sits under 'Holding up' as if these cards had tested it, when none counts money.
screens.instead: Holding up with 7 agents: all 7 had a booking call ring out this week, on a median 6 days out of 7, and none thinks calling back is enough. Seven is few, and the euros are tested in the commercial stage, so read that next before booking pilots.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I can see it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts yes-sayers on a 0-to-7 axis, all 7 cells for me, with my bar marked at 6 (at least 8 in 10), so all three read at first look.
screens.why_b3: The band and the act, a booking call left to ring out in the last 7 days, are mine, but the belief line says only 'reservation agents' and drops 'at hotel groups' and the German central-office or call-center qualifier I typed.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' plus a pointer to the next two cards is a generic hand-off; it doesn't say what this means for the idea, for example that the missed booking call is real even in groups with a call center, so the open question is how much money it costs.
screens.why_b5: n is shown (7 answered, 7 counted) and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than seven people can carry.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 reservation agents at hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center let a booking call ring out in the last 7 days. All 7 did, so the missed call is real even where a call center answers. A lean from 7, not proof. Next, check whether those calls cost bookings worth paying to recover.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 inside what you said · bar 5 of 7" and the median of 6 days, so I can see both the verdict and the count that decides it.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7 and the 7 people are plain, but the axis starts at a 0 nobody could pick, the legend's "what you said" and "at what you said" blur together, and the strip's marker at 5 (people) sits next to my low of 5 (days), so I had to look twice to see which 5 is the bar.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the belief, but I wrote about booking calls that rang out unanswered, and "let a booking call ring out" makes it sound as if my agents chose to ignore guests; the Asked line also repeats "Asked:" and tacks on "the most recent time it happened", which does not fit a count over 7 days.
screens.why_b4: "Whether it matters is the next card" points me onward but says nothing concrete, such as that missed calls happen on most shifts so the forwarding pitch has a daily trigger.
screens.why_b5: The card keeps n visible (7 answered, 7 counted), calls it "a lean, not a call", and claims nothing beyond 6 of 7 against a bar of 5.
screens.instead: Holding up: 6 of 7 agents had a booking call ring out unanswered on 5 or more of the last 7 days (median 6; you needed 5 of 7), so missed calls are a near-daily event worth pitching on, but with only 7 people this is a lean.

screens.why_b1: The status word Holding up sits beside 6 of 7 and the bar of 5 of 7, so I know the result and the number that decides it at once, though the count is printed twice.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 7 people each picked two for 14 picks, my row's 6 stands out against four rivals at 2 each, and the strip turns that into 6 people for and 1 against with the marker at 5, so the count, the n and the bar are all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Importance, and the belief line is my five-item list with Keel's own-row wording, Picking up booking calls in time, which is my missed-call problem as I recognise it.
screens.why_b4: The So line is a reading caution (top two, not first) rather than a next step; it does not say that the one person against works at a group whose call center already covers after hours, which is the segment question I would act on.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible, the count line says this is a lean, not a call, and the So line limits the claim to these 7 and to the top two, so nothing overstates.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much it cleared my bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each person's last callback outcome over 7 people; my line sits under 'Every missed call called back within the hour' with 0 above it, and the strip's marker at 5 against 7 cells is plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Calling back guests whose call rang out' and the five rungs are the ones I saved, my line sits under my own first rung, and the belief reads as mine.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is generic; it never says the gap is callbacks made only 'when there was time', which is exactly what live AI answering of missed calls would close.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen says outright 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so even 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: Say: none of these 7 called every missed guest back within the hour, and 5 of 7 called back only when there was time; that is the gap answering missed calls live must beat in the next study, a lean from 7, not a call. Ask about 'your last shift with a missed call', not 'your last booking call'.

screens.why_b1: The verdict is stated as 'Holding up' and again as 'Importance held, 6 of 7', with the bar of 5 of 7 right beside it, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Importance and the belief line is the one I checked: picking up booking calls in time as one of the two things reservation agents would most like made easier.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what this means for Codyco, for example whether groups whose call center already covers after hours are a weaker segment to pitch.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and the single dissenter stay visible, and nothing is claimed beyond what the seven said.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's quote adds something I didn't write: where a call center already covers the evening, the pain moves to group requests by email with no rates attached, which pushes against my 'even with call centers' line.
screens.instead: Importance held, 6 of 7 against a bar of 5; the one who ranked it lower works where a call center covers after six, and her pain is group emails without rates, so qualify leads by whether evenings are already covered.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks whether I belong in the study, and asking where I work is the obvious way to start before anything about my calls.
screens.why2: Hotel group, central reservations office and call centre are what we call our own setup in Munich, so I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know where I work and that we run a central reservations office, so I answer it at once.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with no overlap, and a gate rightly has no escape.
screens.why5: It repeats the founder's segment almost word for word and tells me nothing about any product.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options that are easy to hold, though §17's plain 'Yes or no.' would sound more natural than 'I'll read 2 options'.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work in a central reservations office, asking whether a booking call went unanswered last week is the obvious first thing to find out.
screens.why2: 'Booking call' and 'ring out unanswered' are how we talk on the floor, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: On a trade-fair Saturday the calls queue on the ACD while I'm on another guest, so I see the waiting count but not whether a particular call rang out on me; the supervisor's abandoned-call report knows that better than I do, so I'd partly guess.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: The founder's point is that not every call gets answered, but 'did you let' makes it sound like my choice or my fault, when really all lines were busy, so it has drifted a little toward blame.
screens.why6: One short question with 'Yes or no' at the end; easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks about the costly event, not the routine; an agent on a quiet shift who picked up every call can truly say No, and one with calls dropping in the queue says Yes, so the share can support or refute the band.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call to you go unanswered? Yes or no.

screens.why1: I just said yes to letting a call ring out this week, so asking on how many days it happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Booking call and ring out unanswered are how we talk on the floor, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: In our central office the system queues and spreads the calls, so on a trade-fair Saturday I see calls stacking on the board and dropping, but I can't always say whether it was me who let one ring out or the queue that lost it, so I'd half-guess.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 with I can't recall apart covers every answer I could give after my yes, and none of the buttons overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder's plan reaches me; it is only about my calls.
screens.why6: One short question, then a number from 1 to 7, then can't recall: easy to hold and answer by ear.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of days in the window, from 1 to 7 with no 0 and with the one escape set apart, and the event is one short act in the past, so a count reads straight against a founder's range in days.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 7 days did a booking call you could have taken ring out before you picked up? 1 to 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking how often my calls rang out, asking which part of a phone shift I would most like made easier follows naturally.
screens.why2: Rebuchungen, rates, group requests and picking up in time are exactly how we talk in the reservations office, and I get it on one hearing.
screens.why3: On a trade-fair Saturday I do all of these myself, so I can answer from my own last shift without guessing.
screens.why4: Most rows are distinct and in my words, but answering group requests by email is inbox work rather than part of a shift on the phones, so it sits oddly beside the rest.
screens.why5: Picking up booking calls in time keeps the founder's verb and moment, and nothing about a product or tool reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question and five short parallel phrases I can hold, with None of these said once at the end.
screens.why7: The founder's own row is there and not first, there are enough rivals, None of these is at the first ask, and the belief can go either way, but the email row drifts to another channel than the phones the anchor names, which bends one rule.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift on the phones. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Handling changes to existing bookings; Picking up booking calls in time; Answering guests' questions about their stay; Quoting the right rate while the guest waits; Taking group bookings over the phone; or None of these.

screens.why1: After saying calls rang out and which part I'd like easier, it makes sense to ask how calling those guests back actually went.
screens.why2: "How did calling back guests whose call rang out go" is a knotted phrase I'd need to hear twice, though "rang out" and "called back" are our own words at the desk.
screens.why3: My last booking call was one call I answered, but the options are about every missed call on a shift, so I'd have to guess which time I'm meant to judge.
screens.why4: "Within the hour" and "all that day" can both be true and measure time, while the lower rungs count how many, and the common case is missing: the guest rang again themselves or booked elsewhere before we could call.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or the founder's own terms reaches me; it's about missed calls and callbacks in plain desk language.
screens.why6: The stem is a mouthful and the first option is long when spoken, though five options plus one escape can be held.
screens.why7: There are working rungs above any line and a fitting escape, but the measure drifts from speed of callback to how many were called back, and the last rung, "simply lost", names an outcome instead of the callback going worse, the card's own spec 226 example.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift on the phones. How many of the calls that rang out did you get back to? All of them the same day; most of them; about half; only a few; none of them -- or say someone else did it.
